country.comment: Single-country municipal-level study of Colombia examining decentralization and Law 142 of 1994 water and sewerage reforms.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title, Summary, and Section 1; PDF p. 2, Section 2

effect_estimate.comment: Note that minus signs are omitted by font encoding in PDF Tables 3-5, so directions of negative coefficients are verified directly against the authors' text in Sections 5-8 (PDF pp. 6-10). Primary WASH outcomes are municipal household water and sewerage coverage; child mortality is the primary health outcome.
effect_estimate.value: In two-period inter-census difference-in-differences models of household service coverage (1993 and 2005 censuses; N = 932 observations across 484 municipalities, Table 5), overall water coverage rose by ~11 percentage points and sewerage coverage by ~9 percentage points, while municipal Law 142 corporatization/privatization reform (transferring provision from the municipality to an EICE or ESP S.A.) increased sewerage coverage by ~4 percentage points relative to unreformed municipalities (FE models: +3.395 pp, SE 1.679, p < 0.05 in Col. 8; +4.292 pp, SE 2.372, p < 0.10 in Col. 10; +4.627 pp, SE 2.414, p < 0.10 in Col. 12), with insignificant interactions for >2,500 subscribers or mixed/private capital. Conversely, for water supply coverage, reformed municipalities with >2,500 subscribers experienced a ~6 to 7.9 percentage point smaller coverage increase than unreformed municipalities (FE models: -7.928 pp, SE 2.331, p < 0.01 in Col. 4; -7.460 pp, SE 2.332, p < 0.01 in Col. 6), and reformed municipalities with mixed or private capital had a 4.5 to 5.2 percentage point smaller water coverage increase (-4.504 pp, SE 2.034, p < 0.05 without FE in Col. 5; -5.230 pp, SE 2.427, p < 0.05 with FE in Col. 6; ~12 pp lower when both features were present). In xtlogit reform-adoption models (N = 2,018 observations across 318 municipalities, Table 3), higher baseline 1993 coverage (+0.0163 to +0.0187, p < 0.05/0.10) and effective number of political parties (+0.330 to +0.344, p < 0.05) increased reform likelihood, whereas electoral turnout (-2.452 to -2.808, p < 0.05) and rurality (-0.0170 to -0.0172, p < 0.10) reduced it. For under-5 infectious-disease mortality (1990-2004 DiD with PS common support, N = 2,386 nonzero observations across 307 municipalities, Table 4 Col. 4), reform alone reduced mortality by 0.0463 percentage points (SE 0.0265, p < 0.10; -0.0733 pp, SE 0.0224, p < 0.01 in full sample N = 3,332 across 380 municipalities), but the interaction with >2,500 subscribers was +0.142 percentage points (SE 0.0342, p < 0.01), yielding a net 0.096 percentage point slower mortality decline in large reformed municipalities relative to direct municipal provision.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Summary; PDF pp. 6-7, Section 5 and Table 3; PDF pp. 8-9, Sections 6-7 and Table 4; PDF p. 10, Section 8 and Table 5

mechanism_certainty.comment: Although appraised with ROBINS-I as a DiD policy evaluation, overall risk of bias is Serious: the water/sewerage coverage DiD model (Equation 3, Table 5) relies on only two census waves (1993 and 2005) with no pre-trend check, omits all time-varying covariates (poverty, fiscal transfers, political competition, turnout) shown in Table 3 to predict reform adoption, and applies no propensity-score trimming despite a 17.5 percentage point baseline water coverage gap between reforming and non-reforming municipalities (78.0% vs. 60.5%, Figure 2), while the infectious-disease mortality regressions drop zero-death municipality-years (conditioning on a post-treatment outcome). Because Serious ROBINS-I risk of bias precludes a rating of 3, and because the study estimates municipal-level statistical associations using provider corporate-form indicators rather than directly observing administrative or household-level institutional mechanisms (explicitly leaving provider incentives and sector policies to future research, PDF p. 10), certainty is coded as 1 (documented statistical association).
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 5, Section 4(a) and Figure 2; PDF pp. 6-10, Sections 5-8 and Tables 3-5

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines municipal statutory autonomy/discretion under Law 60 of 1993 and Law 142 of 1994 (Art. 6) to retain direct municipal provision or transfer service to corporatized public (EICE) or private/mixed (ESP S.A.) utilities (discretion); intergovernmental decentralization, fiscal transfers, and local electoral/party politics shaping service delivery and reform adoption (political_coordination, institutional_fragmentation); citizen oversight provisions and local electoral turnout/public participation modeled in Table 3 (participation); and Colombia's cross-subsidized socioeconomic strata tariff/user-fee system under Law 142 and Laws 60/715 (fees).
